speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. Murphy (Lambton West) moved:
subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO PROMOTE AND ACCELERATE ACTIVITY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, a special committee, representative of all parties, with power
to call witnesses and send for documents and papers, should be appointed for the purpose of examining and reporting upon the advisability of providing inducements to promote and accelerate activities in the field of research.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very happy on this occasion to speak on this subject from this side of the house. As you know, this matter has been of great interest for several years, not only to members of the House of Commons, but to the public in general throughout the country, and I am not overlooking those who are interested in science and research, including those in the research council, universities and different engineering and chemical societies. I have urged in the past, Mr. Speaker, that this committee be set up and given the power to call witnesses other than those on the government payroll.
For the record, I might state now that this subject has been discussed on three different occasions, in 1953-54, in 1955 and in 1956. Committees were set up on three different occasions to study the activities of the atomic energy control board and the national research council. But it was the idea of members of our party that in addition to those representing the atomic energy control board and those from the national research council, we should hear evidence from parties such as presidents of universities, the heads of industries, the heads of labour organizations including labour economists and also those such as Dr. Spinks, Dr. Stratford and others who made representations before the Massey commission some years ago.
It was in 1956 that the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) in discussing this subject also asked for an amendment to a motion which was before the house at that time concerning the national research council act. He asked that the motion be amended in order that we could send for persons, unclassified papers and records. That amendment was defeated in the house by a vote of 72 to 127. As a matter of fact all the members of the Conservative party were supported by the other two minority groups, namely the C.C.F. and the Social Credit. We feel that the committee would serve a much better purpose if it were allowed to call these outside witnesses. I think today research is one of the most important aspects of our economic life.
2250	HOUSE OF
Proposal to Increase Research Activities
I should like now to give the house a definition of research, because it is extremely broad. To me the term "research" is something like the term "time". It is a relevant term. Time may mean a fraction of a second or a millennium. In my opinion-and I think the house will agree with me-the term "research" is equally broad. The Oxford dictionary defines research as the endeavour to discover facts by scientific study of the subjects, which includes innovation, the development of new, better and more efficient ways of doing anything requiring human effort.
This country and the free world today are facing problems that are increasing in their importance, and I refer particularly to inflation. The part I hope to contribute will deal with productivity, in turn relating to research. I have a good example of that, for instance, in my own riding, where we have an extremely high productivity per person. In view of the evidence that has come before our committee on mines, forests and waters, 1 intend to relate something for the consideration of this house. It is in connection with the development of the Athabasca tar sands, something that was announced just a few weeks ago for the first time in Canada by one of our well-known scientists in that particular department. His name is Dr. Convey, who made a great contribution in that committee.
Before I go into that matter I should like to say that in Britain, as I have emphasized on previous occasions, they have a standing committee known as a parliamentary and scientific committee which deals primarily with questions relating to research in that nation. I am not going to repeat what has been said in previous years about the functions of that committee or what it has accomplished, but it is on record in many magazines which contain scientific data, emphasizing the success of that particular committee in Britain and giving that committee credit for bringing Britain out of the unfortunate situation in which she found herself after the second world war.
In former speeches, which I will read as part of the record, to which I know the advisers of the government have access and no doubt have studied, and will study, various representations were made when we argued on behalf of accelerated research in this country, not only in connection with meeting competition at home, but also to meet competition abroad. We have had illustrations of our accelerated research, as a matter of fact, in the agricultural field, in health and in other fields, and these are very important.
Mr. Speaker, on the question of productivity, which I think is very important, I would


now like to refer to a matter which was dealt with by this government just a few days ago when I asked the productivity per person per year in the 20 highest levels in this country. I think this is very pertinent information for this house, because it concerns a very important aspect of our national economy; and as I intend to argue later on, if we are going to beat inflation, which is our main problem in this country and elsewhere in the free world, we must increase productivity.
Before I submit these figures I realize, of course, that industries vary, productivity varies, and we must take all that into consideration. In Sarnia, which is an area which I have the honour to represent, according to the figures tabled by the government our productivity was $1 short of $22,000 per man per year. That is about twice as high as the next city, Beauharnois, which showed $11,000 odd; and the lowest in the 20 was Lachine with $7,153. That is the productivity per man per year. The tabulation also shows the average per capita for one year is $7,000.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that one way to overcome inflation, which is the curse of the free world today, is to increase that productivity. I am not suggesting that it can be done overnight, but I am going to say in all sincerity that there is a responsibility on every Canadian and every person in the free world to do their part in increasing that productivity, thus eliminating the curse of inflation. I say without hesitation that if we all put our shoulders to the wheel, whether we belong to a union or are one of the white collar workers, no matter what position we occupy in this country, if we did a little more and probably earned a little more we would put inflation into the background within weeks.
Mr. Speaker, I am going to refer to an advertisement which appeared in a recent issue of the Saturday Evening Post, I believe about a week ago, inserted I believe by the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company. This is one of the most important advertisements which I have read, and I am going to outline a few of the ideas contained therein. It says that there is a cure for inflation; that even a little inflation is bad. It goes on to say what the government can do. It can pay its current expenses out of its current income. This calls for discipline and courage in government. The article adds, under the subheading "What we can do to help" the following words:
We can urge and actively support economies in government-whether federal, state or local. This does not mean endangering national security or affecting vital services, but it does mean helping the government to limit spending to services which are truly necessary.
Cutting government expenditures is a job for everyone, if taxes and our government debt are

to be reduced. Reduction of both is extremely important in our fight against inflation.
Another paragraph reads:
We can buy prudently. It is always wise to get full value for our money. But, in time of inflation, it is even more important.
But I think the most important part of all is the paragraph which I am now going to read:
We can give a dollar's worth of value for every dollar we earn. Increased productivity is an effective way to help defeat inflation. Here is what President Eisenhower said about productivity :
"... if our efficiency does not increase, if our productivity does not rise, we . . . will tend to fall into the costly error of overpaying ourselves for the work we do. Along that road . . . lies the spur to further inflation."
I should also like to quote an article written by Mr. Solomon Fabricant which I happened to come across a few days ago. The title of the article is "Basic Facts on Productivity Change". It is described as occasional paper No. 63, and it was printed by the National Bureau of Economic Research, Inc., in the United States. I am glad to say we have a representative on that committee. Mr. Fabricant is, I think, one of the best recognized economists in the free world, and here is what he has to say on page 1 of this pamphlet, which was published in 1959:
Productivity deserves the attention that it has received, for it is a measure of the efficiency with which resources are converted into the commodities and services that men want. Higher productivity is a means to better levels of economic wellbeing and greater national strength. Higher productivity is a major source of the increment in income over which men bargain and sometimes quarrel. And	higher-or	lower-productivity
affects costs, prices, profits, output, employment and investment, and thus plays a part in business fluctuations, in inflation, and in the rise and decline of industries.
Indeed, in one way or another, productivity enters virtually every broad economic problem, whatever current form or new name the problem takes-industrialization, or research and development, or automation, or tax reform, or cost-price squeeze, or improvement factor, or wage inflation, or foreign dollar shortage.
Productivity, as I think every member of the house would agree, is clearly allied with research, and we have contended in the past it is the responsibility of government to take the lead in accelerating research in this country in order that we may be better equipped to meet competition, particularly from abroad. In addition, as I have already emphasized, it has an important part to play in curbing the inflationary spiral.
I remember asking in the course of one of the speeches I made some years ago whether we were doing enough in the field of research in Canada, and the questions I asked in those days-and they were asked

Proposal to Increase Research Activities by other members of this party besides myself-are even more important today than they were at that time. In the interval we have witnessed the arrival of the sputnik, a 1957 scientific venture of such importance that I do not think anything has excelled it during the last century.
I should like now to refer to our position in research with respect to what is taking place in our northland, the part of Canada which lies north of the mainland in the Arctic regions. I also intend to refer to the tar sands, because this subject was before the committee to which I have referred, and Dr. Convey made the startling statement that the tar sands in that area, which cover some 17,000 square miles, contain as much as 300 billion barrels of oil.
That is an astronomical figure. It is probably two and one half times the known resources of the remainder of the free world. If we calculate it according to the estimate of one barrel per cubic yard, the figure would be twice as great. In terms of dollars and cents, Mr. Speaker, that is well over $900 billion, if we use the figures of Dr. Convey. This is another figure which is almost beyond the comprehension of the human brain and it is something that we in Canada can be very proud of because we are very fortunate in having so many metals. I submit that now we must find greater use for many of those metals because we are finding, through research, that plastic is taking the place of lead, and so on. We have our gold lying underground instead of being used.
I want to relate what I mentioned a moment ago to the Athabasca tar sands. There have been some eight underground explosions in the United States, and as a result of those explosions it has been decided that the Richfield Oil Corporation, in conjunction with other interests, will make a similar test in Alberta which they expect will be successful. It is claimed by the scientists that they can now separate the sand from the oil which will again, as I say, be a tremendous benefit not only to this country but to the free world.
The point I am coming to, Mr. Speaker, is this. It is proposed that in this-I will not call it an experiment though in a way it is- there will be associated the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Department of National Health and Welfare, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, the Alberta research council, the Alberta conservation board for gas and oil, the Richfield Oil Corporation and also the United States atomic energy group. I mentioned a moment ago that this technical group includes representatives from the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, and I believe our atomic energy board will be represented as well.
2252	HOUSE OF
Proposal to Increase Research Activities
Here we have a huge enterprise far surpassing anyone's imagination, with a potential which may be the greatest asset the free world has ever known and, according to our information at the moment, we in this country are going to rely entirely on United States research methods and application. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the recovery of the oil is to be brought about by exploding small atomic bombs some 1,200 or 2,000 feet below the ground, as the case may be, or some 200 feet below the tar sands. I was hoping to get information before I spoke today as to the number of bombs that would be required. They claim that this is going to be a successful operation. My submission is that we in this country should now accept our responsibilities as one of the foremost members of the commonwealth and establish our own separation plants in Canada for the purpose of doing in Canada the work that was proposed to be done by the atomic energy board of the United States.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that it was said in this house some years ago by the then minister of trade and commerce that we could make atomic bombs. We are still interested in using atomic energy for peaceful purposes by making bombs in this country. We now make cobalt and other bombs and we use isotopes for agricultural, medical and other purposes. Because we have probably the second largest known uranium ore bodies in the world-I think South Africa is first; as I recall the figures I think we produce about 30 per cent of the world's total-this project could be undertaken in this country.
It will be an expensive project. I noticed a proposal in the press on Saturday by the present president of Rio Tinto. He is calling for a joint federal-provincial research program of sufficient magnitude to assure Canada's position in the nuclear energy field. He believes that both the federal and provincial governments can count on the assistance of private industry. I assume he is referring to the uranium industry, which is a big industry in this country and still in its infancy. Therefore I suggest to the government in all sincerity that this is a new approach, a Canadian approach, to develop our uranium industry more or less independently of any foreign country but still within the British commonwealth of nations.
I make that suggestion because the development involved would require so many millions of dollars and so much export of plutonium and the other by-products that it would probably necessarily mean an association with the commonwealth, and our best customer which would be the United Kingdom. I see no reason, therefore, why this


idea cannot be explored now, not next year, to see whether or not this industry can be developed in Canada in conjunction with the private uranium interests-and their supply is huge-together with the financial assistance and co-operation of the United Kingdom. This may involve the expenditure of $750 million. I am simply drawing this figure out of a hat, but from what I know of the expenditures involved in the United States and elsewhere in developing fissionable products with a separation unit or industry, it would involve probably that amount of money or even more.
I say in all sincerity that we are just at the morning, you might say, of the atomic era. Now is the time for us to accept the challenge. The situation in the world being what it is today, I have no doubt that in this country this industry and this idea will receive favourable support. I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce has reviewed this idea personally, and I hope that before too long, before this operation takes place in the Athabasca tar fields, we can have the program under way. We know that uranium will be purchased under an agreement with the United States for some three or four years more, but we should not have this uncertainty in the business field. I think there is some uncertainty, though most of us cannot help but see a great future for the uranium industry in the development of atomic power for peaceful purposes.
Together with the idea of developing atomic energy for peaceful purposes we could have small nuclear power projects for use in this country and also for export. We may also be able to export these fissionable materials to other than commonwealth countries. I want to say here that I regret, as I think most people do, that we are handicapped in our ability to obtain valuable information from the United States because of legislative enactments made some few years ago in that country. As a result primarily of the espionage and spy trials in Canada the United States has not seen its way clear to share much of its information on matters having to do with fission with Great Britain and Canada in particular. I regret this situation, because after all we are in a great partnership, a partnership so important that it must not be allowed to break up; otherwise the security of the free world is in danger.
I have mentioned the oil and tar sands. Canada is engaged in the oil and gas industry, and research is so applicable to that industry. No country in the world today can surpass the reserves of oil and gas that we have. We are in a most enviable position, and I think most members will agree that in the days to come a great deal of our research will be in the petrochemical industry. We in Canada

have a high cost economy, but because a smaller amount of manpower is required in the petrochemical industry we can develop that industry successfully. Its development is only in its infancy. Up to now oil and gas have only been discovered in one part of our country and, unfortunately, not in other parts. Therefore it is going to cost something to transport these products.
So far as oil and gas are concerned, the important thing the government has under consideration at the moment is the setting up of an energy board. This is more important today than it ever was in the history of Canada, because this is the most important industry in Canada today. In the early days we had an agricultural economy, in later days a sharing of the economy by industry, but in the days to come I think our big development will be in the petrochemical field. As I said before, and it is worth repeating, we are in the enviable position of having such huge reserves of oil and gas. One reason there is such high productivity in Sarnia is that it is a petrochemical area. There are other areas in Canada, such as Montreal, which can be equally important because they must get their end products from gasoline or oil as the case may be.
I want to mention here that some time ago a few members of parliament went to Sarnia with me and visited the Polymer Corporation plant and some of the other chemical plants. They were astonished to find that the new Imperial Oil petrochemical plant, which cost approximately $30 million, is operated by eight men on a shift or 24 men to cover three shifts a day. That does not include maintenance men. We did not see any there that day, because it is a new plant and the number of maintenance men will be very few. I mention that as an example of an astonishing development through research, a development that means a great deal to the economy of Canada because we must increase our productivity. Automation has been under way for years. In my view it will be accelerated, because only through such acceleration can we have increased productivity.
There is another point I should like to mention. It concerns our situation in Canada, of having industries whose parent companies are in the United States or Great Britain. During the same tour to which I have referred we also went through the Dow Chemical plant, which cost $75 million to $90 million. The vice president took us on a tour of the plant, and I was very glad to hear him tell the members of the House of Commons who were present that the Dow Chemical plant had more Ph.D.'s than any other industry in Canada. I never realized that before, though I knew they had a large, highly 66968-9-143
Proposal to Increase Research Activities trained technical staff of engineers and others with higher training. To me that meant only one thing; it meant that in Sarnia there was a research laboratory that I had not realized was as important as it is.
That brings me to this point. Since discussions about research and the necessity of accelerated research first started in this country a number of plants have set up research divisions. Incidentally, I had the honour of being present when some of these laboratories were opened. I am only going to mention a few of them. In the last few years research divisions have been opened by Dupont, C.I.L., Shawinigan Chemicals, Polymer, Imperial Oil, Dow Chemical, Consolidated Mining and Smelting, Canadian Chemicals, International Nickel and others. Perhaps some hon. members have read the statement received in the mail this morning from Imperial Oil, or will read the one which I hope will come to hand within a few days from the Polymer Corporation. Former Polymer reports prove conclusively to anyone interested in reading them that the success of that huge crown corporation has been the result of research, and that industry certainly has an excellent research team.
-I mentioned a while ago that Dow Chemical was apparently doing more research than I thought was the case. I want to suggest now that many more United States industries with branch plants in Canada could well establish research divisions in this country, staffed with Canadian workers, in the same way Dow Chemical has done. I wish to give some reasons why United States industries could well consider establishing research divisions in this country. In the first place, the cost in Canada is lower. Unfortunately the salaries of Canadian scientists are not as high as the salaries of scientists in the United States, with the result that the cost of research is lower in Canada.
We welcome United States and other foreign capital to this country to aid in our development. We do not have the money to develop our country. We have the resources, and I submit that if United States industries would establish research laboratories in this country, as has been advocated over the years in practically every speech in the house on this subject, it would bring about better relationships.
I know that there are some who think there is too much United States investment in Canada. I do not agree with that view, and I do say that greater participation in research programs by Canadian subsidiaries of United States companies would make for better relationships.
Public relations is a very important aspect of the association of any two countries, and
2254	HOUSE OF
Proposal to Increase Research Activities especially our two countries because of the differences which have arisen as the result of quotas on many of our agricultural products as well as lead and zinc. Lead and zinc are perhaps not so important today as they were some years ago. The demand for copper is growing. Plastics are replacing some of the other base metals, and no doubt research will develop other uses for these products in the future.
There is another reason, and that is this would permit beneficial research work to be carried out in secluded spots. It is not necessary to have a research laboratory located at the back door or front door of an industry. In fact the best work is done by scientists who are remote from the industry. They are not the type of men who are going to punch a time clock. A research division could well be established in this country 500 or 1,000 miles away from the parent industry. This plan would make use of engineers who might be barred, because of quota restrictions, from entering the United States but who could be admitted to Canada.
I feel, therefore, that further representations could be made with a view to encouraging United States industries to set up research divisions in Canada. United States participation in our economic life is here and is here to stay. It is becoming more important every day. In order to make this participation more Canadian, these industries must take part in the fundamental approaches to our problems.
I am going to say now, Mr. Speaker, that since the government has been the major spender of funds in this field more stress should be laid upon research contracts, whether they be with industries or universities. I have maintained in the past that every campus should have a research team. Then those who want to obtain a greater amount of detailed knowledge in any particular field will go to the particular university in Canada specializing in that field. We have not had that situation in Canada, I am sorry to say. This fact was borne out three or four years ago when a team from a well known organization in Britain visited our universities and came to the conclusion that this country needed advancement in that particular field.
I do not believe the government should employ universities to do applied research. If that has been the practice in the past I do hope that in future this field will be left to industry.
I must say here, Mr. Speaker, and I regret not having said it earlier in my remarks, that I should like to pay high tribute to our scientists and engineers in the national research council and in the atomic energy field


at Chalk River. I was fortunate enough to be a member of the committee that visited Chalk River and, as a layman, I must say it required hours of intensive study to glean even the faintest idea of the job they were doing. This was one of the most interesting committees of which I have ever been a member. I am hoping, of course, that we will have another one, because it is important that the people of this country know what the government is doing, and know why so much money has to be appropriated for this purpose. As the years go by much more money is going to be required, not only by government but by industry as well to accelerate and promote research in this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be much easier to speak to this resolution if it were couched in more specific terms. The resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, a special committee, representative of all parties, with power to call witnesses and send for documents and papers, should be appointed for the purpose of examining and reporting upon the advisability of providing inducements to promote and accelerate activities in the field of research.
The operational words in this resolution would appear to be "the advisability of providing inducements". Now, so far as the idea of increasing and accelerating research is concerned, I am sure everybody in this house would be entirely in favour of that. If special inducements were required to bring this about then that, too, I am sure would receive hearty support from all sides of this house. Why this committee should need the power to send for documents and papers to achieve this objective is a little beyond my comprehension.
Specifically, the resolution calls for a committee to seek ways and means of increasing our research facilities. As I said, no one could quarrel with that objective, and I am sure every member in every part of this house will support it wholeheartedly. However, this resolution presupposes that we are not now doing as much as we ought, and that point I think is debatable. Research facilities are very costly, and what a country like Canada can afford to provide in that respect is limited by our population and by the financial resources we can allocate to that specific activity.
We must bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that we have a national research council which has done excellent work and has made a contribution to the world of science of which Canada can very well be proud. We think of the research work that has been done with

respect to the Arctic; the development of Arctic clothing for our troops; buildings for the Arctic. Then there was the atomic reactor at Chalk River which was a pioneer venture in that line, and the cobalt bomb. These are notable contributions which I think stand out all the more as Canadian contributions in view of the limited resources at our disposal.
Then we have the fisheries research board. While this body works very quietly and perhaps does not make the headlines, the fisheries research board is doing commendable work in exploring new types of fishing equipment and in finding ways and means of packaging and processing our fish in order to lower handling costs. In addition we have the Connaught laboratories. In that connection we can take pride in the contribution made through the discovery of insulin and more recently in the development of the Salk vaccine. Over the week end I was told, I do not know how true this is, that there were news reports to the effect that some Canadian scientist had developed a process for separating strontium 90 from calcium. I have not had the opportunity of verifying that report, but if it is a fact then that is a contribution which I believe the whole world will applaud.
I think the future health of our children and the effects of atomic fall-out are subjects which occupy the minds of people living everywhere, in all civilized countries. Then we have some research going on at various universities all across Canada. I think it was at McGill University that Dr. Rutherford first carried out the experiment which laid the foundation of nuclear physics. On top of that we have a fair amount of industrial research being carried out by private enterprise. Hence the amount of research already going on in Canada at the present time is not inconsiderable.
The resolution presupposes that this amount is not enough. Of course if we can find ways and means of improving our research facilities increasing the number of projects or providing new ideas for research, the committee will make a useful contribution. Certainly I cannot see how such a committee can possibly do any harm.
The resolution states that the purpose of the committee would be "to promote and accelerate activities in the field of research". Mr. Speaker, there are many fields of research. I presume that what this resolution means is that the purpose would be to promote research generally. I would prefer that the resolution pinpointed certain projects upon which the committee might concentrate. What I have in mind is research carried out to try to find solutions to our great national problems. At the present time we have several 66968-9-143i

Proposal to Increase Research Activities national problems. We have a tremendous wheat surplus. We have a coal surplus in Nova Scotia. That coal cannot be sold economically in competition with coal from other countries. In my own province and along the Atlantic seaboard we have tremendous fish resources which do not yield a profitable return to the producer.
It seems to me that one of the answers to these problems must lie in the development of new products from these sources. If we could only find a way of using half our wheat surplus in order to produce some other product, our agricultural problem would be solved. If we could find ways and means of developing new products from our Nova Scotia coal the problem of the coal mines in Nova Scotia would be solved. If we could develop products such as plastics from our fish products in Newfoundland, our fishing industry would be much better off. If such a committee were set up, Mr. Speaker, I think these are the specific avenues to which I should like to see some attention directed.
The hon. member has laid great stress on productivity as a cure for inflation. I am afraid I cannot agree with him there. We have always increased our productivity, whether little or much; sometimes it has been 2 per cent and sometimes it has been 4 per cent, but an increase in productivity has not had much effect on inflation. Even if we could increase our productivity tenfold, unless the benefit of that productivity was passed along to the consumer I cannot see how it could possibly have any effect at all on the problem of inflation.
I would therefore make this suggestion. Before we set up a committee to seek ways and means of increasing research facilities or of developing some form of inducement- because all this procedure is going to cost money-it might perhaps be wiser if the committee confined its activities to finding ways and means of consolidating and co-ordinating the research facilities we already have. I believe there is room there for thought. In a country like Canada, with such a variety of interests, such a variety of climatic conditions and such a variety of natural resources, it is difficult to co-ordinate research projects and it is quite easy for unnecessary duplication to exist.
I should therefore think that the first duty of this committee would be to assess the facilities that we already have, and to seek ways and means of consolidating them in order to avoid any overlapping. Mr. Speaker,
I am very happy to support the resolution of the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy). To my mind this is one of the most important resolutions which could be placed before the house. The whole subject with which it deals in rather large and general terms is to my mind again one field which perhaps has more potential for contribution by this government and by the actions of such a committee than almost any other field that we could investigate and embark upon.
Of course, a resolution of this type and nature has been before the house for several years, and I feel that every member in the house must congratulate the hon. member for Lambton West on his interest and tenacity in pursuing this subject. It is one which is perhaps controversial only to a degree; I would say, to the extent one carries out investigations into research itself or the extent of government aid to research. We can see this generally in the speeches that have gone immediately before from the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). I would just comment, however, that the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo in his remarks, with which I would generally agree, was negative; the tenor of his remarks was negative. He said he could not see how this committee could possibly do any harm. That might be true, but I think it is a rather negative observation on the tremendous need we have in Canada to study and to accelerate this whole process of research.

Proposal to Increase Research Activities
I would also add that several of our present cabinet ministers have spoken on this resolution in the past and supported it actively in the years when they were in opposition. I would strongly urge that action on this committee be taken, and that the government set it up as reasonably soon as possible. There is a counterpart of this committee in Great Britain. There they have a very interesting committee which has had a most useful effect over the last few years. It is called the parliamentary and scientific committee.
The first one was founded in 1939 and it included members of all parties of the House of Commons of Great Britain. It replaced at that time the former parliamentary science committee. The present committee in Great Britain is one of a number of informal parliamentary groups. Incidentally, membership is open to members of parliament and to nominated representatives from various other institutions such as universities and other non-profit institutions. This standing committee, acting as it does on a regular basis, provides an interchange of most important information, a constant interchange of information between those trained scientists and the members of parliament, or those people, in other words, who are legislating upon matters which must inevitably affect the growth of scientific progress in any country.
This is something which I believe is called for here, although the structure of our committee might be somewhat different. It is something that we very much need in Canada and it is something which this resolution calls for. I think the need for research in Canada is unquestioned. We have a history of research going back many years, but it has been the experience of all countries of the world that almost inevitably governments, either federal or provincial, as we have them in Canada, have had an ever increasing part to play in the fostering and advancing of research.
In the general sense of scientific and fundamental social research it has been the feeling that these are fields which it has not appeared wise to leave entirely to industry or to universities. They are fields which need some co-ordination in research and in many instances it comes down to matters of finance from governments. I think this is particularly true in Canada today. We are a small nation of some 17 million people; we are a trading nation, tremendously dependent upon export and we are a nation facing the problem, as the hon. member for Lambton West mentioned, of productivity and ever-increasing costs and the problems of competition,
2260	HOUSE OF
Proposal to Increase Research Activities competition within North America and competition all around the world.
This puts a premium on research in Canada. We do not have the great internal markets which many nations such as the United States, for instance, have, and which cushion them somewhat against costs. All of which creates a need for greater ingenuity with which to produce industrial products. This, of course, is just one aspect, the economic aspect, of fundamental research and applied research, and the eifect which it must have on each and every one of us in the products we buy and their relative costs. Because of the position in which we now find ourselves Canada should probably be in the very forefront of research expenditure on a per capita basis. Probably there should be a premium placed on our ability in Canada today to use our ingenuity, our research establishments and our brain power to make up for the problems we have in a widely scattered population and the heavy costs which they generally incur.
We have as well the tremendous defence problems with which the free world and we in North America are faced. These problems of defence are dependent, of course, partially upon scientific research. We have our own defence research board, of course. This is a fundamental problem and one which is typical today. We have seen, of course, in the last two or three years particularly, that defence can shade almost imperceptibly into economic defence as well. In other words, defence research may be connected partially with producing products in a more imaginative fashion and at lower costs to compete in the economic structure which we are facing more and more in this world and which is allied to our military defence problem. The threats that we have been facing from Russia are a culmination of those two facts, with the problem of economic defence or offence thereby causing our research interests to come to the forefront more and more in the last two or three years.
This committee would be a tremendously important thing in Canada. It could gather together from all across our land leaders in the scientific world, leaders in industrial research, people from various government departments, many of whom are now engaged in fundamental and applied research and, I think perhaps most important of all, leaders from our universities across Canada, those institutions which to my mind must be the bulwark and the foundation of fundamental research in this country.
We have faced in Canada this growing need for additional research and we have been feeling our way, so to speak, into the


interrelationship between the various parties involved in this problem. By "interrelationship", of course, I mean our federal and provincial governments, our various educational institutions, our industries and other groups of that nature. I should like to treat this interrelationship as a part of the problem which this committee, if set up, would study, because while I feel that financial aid is, of course, a most important necessity on the part of the federal government, I think that can only be carried out as a result of concurrent studies of the interrelationship of our various research organizations. They are complex. They have grown gradually as is natural with a small country, but they have now increased to a fair size and complexity and perhaps there are changes to be made which might be of great advantage.
Before the first world war Canada was engaged in a very moderate amount of research in various places. We were then and are still to a certain extent a country of tremendous natural resources and the problems then wrere more those involving engineering advances, transportation, power and utilities. The focus was more on moulding our vast raw resources into a coherent whole which could make this country function as a unit. We are still, of course, particularly in view of our emphasis on our north country, faced with the problem of the heavy structural integration of Canada as a whole.
The first world war brought up a number of interesting matters and one might say that it more or less started the Canadian government on the road to its role in research. This came about in 1916, I believe, when the Canadian government and the government of Great Britain, incidentally, set up very similar groups to study research in their respective countries. At that time the Canadian government created a cabinet committee of six ministers and on their recommendation an honorary advisory council for scientific and industrial research was established. From that we have seen the rise of the present national research council.
The background of development in Great Britain is rather interesting. It came about partially because of the tremendous industrial surge of Germany, the government of that country having taken a very active part in fostering research before the first world war. In Great Britain this had been done to a limited extent but research had largely been in the field of the various learned societies such as the royal society and the royal institute of London. The German government, however, played a very active part and the results of its active participation in research were reflected in

German industry. We saw there at that time a very rapid technological build-up.
Partly as a result of this there was considerable stimulus in Great Britain and Canada toward the formation of a committee which would involve the government more in productive research. The setting up of the national research council after that time grew out of the cabinet committee and in 1928 the government started the erection of a national research council laboratory which was opened in 1932.
In the following years until 1939 or 1940, research activity on the part of the government grew slowly but at the time of the second world war there was a tremendous expansion in this field. Throughout the second world war various laboratories across the country, including several here in Ottawa, were engaged in defence research. This was still within the scope of the national research council and the effort during those war years was naturally of a more applied nature having in mind technological advances, the solving of various problems and successes which could contribute directly to our war effort. Some of the matters one might mention which were the subject of research were various medical fields, radar, biological warfare and so forth. Those are some that come to mind.
However, after the war it became obvious that the defence part should probably have a separate entity, and separate representation. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that the whole structure and interrelationship of the defence research board as it came into being and that of the national research council and other organizations would bear close scrutiny by such a committee as it is proposed should be established. The encouragement of research by additional funds must be related to the structure and interrelationships of the various bodies now engaged in fundamental research.
The defence research board was created shortly after the second world war and was set up in much the same manner as the national research council, with which I should like to deal again in a few moments. Representatives of each of the armed services are members of the board and at the present time, as well as over the past few years, there is considerable interlocking of membership with the national research council. However, structurally the defence research board is a unit and entity within the Department of National Defence.
The defence research board has made a very considerable contribution to research in this country. It gives grants in aid of research to universities and operates as well
Proposal to Increase Research Activities an extensive system of laboratories throughout the country. Much of its research, of course, has been devoted to applied work of direct interest to the armed forces. One can think of laboratories such as that at Suffield, Alberta, the northern laboratory at Churchill, Manitoba, the medical laboratory in Toronto and the armament and research development centre at Quebec city as examples of the places at which these activities are carried out. While in the defence research board the emphasis has been on applied research, there has been considerable success as well with fundamental work, some of it carried out at universities.
The national research council was the predecessor of the defence research board, from which the latter split off as a separate group. The national research council consists at the present time of some 21 members, four of whom are paid officials. The remaining 17 are selected from the universities and industry. I would suggest that a number of these people be interviewed by the committee and be asked to present their thoughts on Canadian research because I think that in a general way their experience is probably more widespread in the field of Canadian research than is the case with the members of any other single group.
The president of the national research council presides over the council and is also in charge of the laboratories which the council operates. Three vice-presidents, paid officials of the council, are responsible for administration, medical research and science respectively. The national research council is not a government department but a separate organization which has the responsibility of the operation of its own laboratories and for assistance to scientific and engineering departments of Canadian universities in pursuing research work. The council, as members know, reports to the committee of the cabinet and it is the chairman of this committee, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), who presents the council's budget to parliament.
It might be said that aid from the national research council to universities for research is substantially greater than that from any other Canadian body. These funds for research are devoted to both fundamental and applied research. There are various scientific divisions within the national research council such as applied biology, pure and applied physics, and pure and applied chemistry. Those are some of the divisions that come readily to mind. Laboratories are not operated by the council in the field of medical research. The vice president

Proposal to Increase Research Activities in charge of this subject works with universities and other institutions in this particular field. The vice president in charge of medical research also presides over the medical committee which recommends awards and scholarships to be made in the medical field.
There are as well, and I think this is an interesting point, some 28 associate committees of the national research council for the purpose of planning programs of research and education as well as bringing into these committees representatives of the various government departments, universities and industries which are directly involved in research.
Of course, one would be remiss if he did not mention nuclear research in Canada. This, in many of its aspects, is again the outgrowth of work done by the national research council. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, a crown company, grew out of the work that had been done some 10 years previously in the national research council. This crown company collaborates with industry in the development and use of atomic energy. We have, as well, the atomic energy control board which handles the distribution of radioactive materials in Canada and awards grants in aid for research in this field to various educational institutions.
I should like to go back for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to the question of where we go from here, particularly as that question relates to the national research council. As I said before, I feel that the universities should be the mainstay of fundamental research in Canada. I feel, not being critical of the council as such, that we have a basic problem of organization in that we have a unit which is both running laboratories on its own, with a very considerable staff, which has considerable investment and production interest, and which is also granting funds for similar or different research to other institutions, mainly universities. This dual role is perhaps a difficult one, perhaps an unwise one, for an institution or a council to be undertaking. I would say, however, it was probably a natural procedure. However, the question arises as to whether or not these roles would be better separated in the future.
We have, as an example, in Great Britain, the formation of three councils. These councils are the medical research council of Great Britain; the agricultural research council of Great Britain; and the department of scientific and industrial research, which is actually a government department and takes up, so to speak, the other areas of industrial and technical research, general biological, physical and chemical research. There are,


in this way, three divisions and not the one organization as we have at present in the national research council. These three organizations report directly to the cabinet. I think that possibly this is a move which might be studied by this committee, if it were set up. Advice could be sought on this question from the people in industry, from the members of the national research council themselves, from the scientists in various government departments engaged in research as well as from the people in universities who are the recipients of a considerable proportion of the money which the national research council grants each year.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that the increase in the funds* for the national research council has been a very encouraging sign. We can scan the expenditures of the national research council and find that in the year 1952-53, for example, $15,400,000 were expended, and much the same in the following 2 years. Coming along to 1955-56, we find that just over $16 million were expended; 1957-58, $20.2 million. Then we see, in the estimates for 1958-59 and 1959-60 very significant increases. In 1958-59 the figure is $25,992,000, while in 1959-60 the figure is $30,133,000. This is a very rapid rate of increase and is, I believe, an important sign of the increasingly important place given to research in this country. I feel that one of the most important points in this connection is that the larger proportion, perhaps 75 per cent or more, of the budget each year is spent on the council's own laboratories, staff and research work. The remainder is used for grants in aid of research and scholarships to universities.
The amount spent on these grants in aid of research and scholarships has jumped very appreciably in the last two years. We had an item in the estimates last year, 1958-59, of almost $6 million for scholarships and grants in aid of research, while in 1959-60 this item has risen to $7,957,000, an increase of $2 million in that period. This money goes largely to our educational institutions. We do not have in these institutions a separate body of research workers but instead, a constantly growing and self-perpetuating body of graduate students, teachers and others who are encouraging and engaging in research. This is a fundamentally sound point about which the people in the research fields across Canada feel rather strongly. It is unwise to separate, to put a wall around a research institution, aside from certain ones connected with defence work, and lose close communication with educational and teaching institutions such as our universities.

This is an important matter. I believe that research should be connected with the universities and educational institutions as much as possible. I would advocate, Mr. Speaker, that this committee might examine the British scheme. As the hon. member for Lambton West mentioned, research groups could be attached to universities across Canada. I can think of no country that would benefit more from the establishment of specialized teams. For example, these people could look into certain aspects of biological, medical, or chemical research and other fields. We, in Canada, can rarely afford the manpower, or the finances of having more than one of these highly specialized groups, but perhaps a council could formulate a plan whereby we could overcome this fundamental problem which we have in Canada today by encouraging research groups.
In many of our specialized fields we simply do not have in Canada adequate facilities for training. A university by itself can generally afford-speaking financially and also in a manpower sense-one man and one man only who is a specialist, let us say, in the diseases of fish, and this subject is used just as an example. It is necessary to give training to graduate students and personnel in universities in order that we can have these people trained and employed in Canada. The need is great. There is a crying need in many fields. With these research groups, one group per specialized field, so to speak, and many of these groups attached to our educational institutions right across Canada, we could give training in depth of knowledge. I think this would be a tremendous step forward in the way of progress.
I might add while mentioning the establishment of a separate medical research council, that a committee headed up by Doctor Farquharson of the university of Toronto, vice president of the national research council in charge of medical research is now studying organization problems. This committee established by the Minister of Trade and Commerce is investigating this whole situation, and should report sometime in the near future.
The small research groups which have played such an important part in general research in Great Britain would be one of the important matters that we should deal With. I would think that this committee, should be one which would first of all make an over-all survey of existing research in Canada, look at the over-all picture first of all and see what areas are most in need of federal assistance or federal reorganization of bodies which come under our jurisdiction. But the committee after that could go on

Proposal to Increase Research Activities as a continuing group which each year during the sessions of parliament or perhaps at other times than during the sessions of parliament could continue to study the various aspects of research in Canada and keep the members of this house up-to-date on the various specialized fields. There is a gap- and I think this gap probably widens each year-between technological and scientific research advances which have made our world almost a wonderland, and our knowledge of them; our ability to legislate in the fields- because we must deal and grapple with these problems-has not increased to a comparative degree. There is a liaison gap there which this committee could fill and where it could play a part which would be of tremendous importance in the years ahead.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss if I were not to mention some other research which is going on in Canada at the present time. We have various government departments, of course, engaged in the field of research. The Department of Fisheries has a fisheries research board, with stations on the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts, and another station, I believe, in the province of Quebec. The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has a mines laboratory. The Department of National Health and Welfare maintains laboratories generally for the protection of public health. The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources has a forest research division and a forest products laboratory. We have seen these various areas of research. One can also add to this the various provincial institutions which are engaged in research, largely applied to industry, particularly industries in the provinces concerned. The federal Department of Agriculture sponsors a great deal of important research. We have seen the reorganization of the federal Department of Agriculture. I refer to the reorganization of the experimental farm services and the science service portion of that department. I think this is a natural outflow of the interrelationships which come about in research. In this day and age one cannot be, let us say, a wheat plant breeder without some knowledge of plant pathology, genetics, soils and so on. The various departments which had been separated and are being brought together in this reorganization scheme provide an example within the Department of Agriculture of an over-all reorganization and channelling of information and research. We should look at this example when studying research in this country. The Department of Agriculture for many years has carried on much useful research in Canada. Probably one could look again at our universities. I have mentioned that the universities are the main stage of

But again in this small country of ours we face a problem. Many of our large companies, those most able to conduct research, are subsidiaries, so to speak, in many cases, of parent companies in Great Britain or in the United States, and the research activities have been carried out by those parent companies to the detriment, perhaps, of research in Canada; certainly to the detriment of the development of personnel and institutions within the particular industry in Canada.

I am not certain as to the situation, Mr. Speaker, but it would be interesting to know in how many cases that five per cent of taxable income deduction for research purposes was made use of by various industrial companies. Two or three years ago the industrial foundation on education was organized. I think there is here a potential opportunity for small companies and medium-size companies with related interests to band together and form research organization. I believe there are one or two of these in existence in Canada at this moment. They have been a very successful part of the research scene in Great Britain, where they receive government encouragement and some government assistance. In various cases industrial or trade groups could join together and pool some of their resources, within the framework of competitive industries, in order to solve a number of research problems so as to make better products or increase productivity. This then, is the research scene as I see it in Canada at the moment. I think that a first and long step forward would be the establishment of this committee of the House of Commons, to examine the whole of the research

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the splendid address made by the mover of this motion and I, like those who have gone before me, would like to congratulate him for his long-standing interest in this subject of such vital importance to Canada, to its parliament and to its people. I know that for many years the hon. member has pioneered in this particular arena in presenting his views and calling for greater consideration of the question.
I have listened with great interest to the most comprehensive coverage of the question of research presented by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Best). I, in my turn, should like to address a few remarks to you, sir, on the question of research as it affects the field of the social sciences. I may say that if my remarks are brief, such brevity is not at all proportionate to my interest in this great question and to the heartiness of my support of the resolution before us. I was quite interested in the discussion of the hon. member who preceded me dealing with the subject of industrial research and technological and technical research. All of this is of tremendous importance, and in the fast-moving world in which we now live we have daily reminders of the vital importance of this very question. There are some who say that international competition and conflict at the present time may appear occasionally to be due to something which is taking place in the classrooms or the research laboratories of various nations. But while that is of tremendous importance, I think we must also regard those matters which are not of a technical nature. I was most impressed to read in the first annual report of the Canada Council words to which I subscribe wholeheartedly:
The country's surging growth, with the promise oii still greater prosperity and even more leisure, poses its own problems. Life and business are likely to become more complex. People will need more "know-how" in industry and business and also greater skill to manage themselves, to enjoy their leisure, to control their environment and to use their machines. All this points to the need for more education-more training of engineers, scientists, and business men, of course-but also for greater numbers of inspired and talented teachers, of artists, humanists and social scientists, and of thinkers of every sort.
Material prosperity alone will not make a great nation. As we press on to push back the frontiers

of material progress, we must aim to advance on the spiritual front, and advance in our artistic expression as a nation.
I agree with the preceding speakers who emphasized and underscored the need for encouragement and advancement of research, which the proposed committee would undertake. But I believe that in the field of social sciences the need is even more acute. In this field few institutions are engaged other than the universities. I was much impressed when the member for Halton pointed out that the fundamental role must be played by the universities, and I think too that it is only in a limited area that the research function can be totally separated from a teaching function.
I was impressed when the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) told us about the increasing research programs of various business corporations. I think this is all to the good, but in the field of social sciences, except for economics and perhaps for those fields of psychology related to personnel management, the burden is left almost completely to the universities. When we consider the need for the furthering of research facilities we must look to the existing functions, roles and opportunities of our Canadian universities. Surely in this field we find very little room for complacency. We find that university faculties are overworked, with too many classes and too little time for research. They use the expression in universities that the head of the department holds the chair in that subject. One Canadian university professor said that he had not a chair but a settee, since he headed three departments and taught four different subjects.
We find, too, that equipment is inadequate and that it is difficult to meet the ordinary demands of the undergraduate population which is ever increasing in these times. You cannot carry on social science research without an adequate library, to say the least. You find, too, that the trained minds who must carry out research in the field of social science are troubled by economic considerations which limit their usefulness in the research aspect of their work. Many university professors instead of pursuing a research program during the vacation period find it necessary to engage in the rather arduous and onerous duties of teaching summer school. When I refer to this question, I am not speaking academically; I understand from personal experience just what is involved. Often the sabbatical leave arrangements are very inadequate. Sometimes the grants which are given are given reluctantly and niggardly, if at all.
Now may I go to something which the hon. member for Halton touched on when he spoke for other areas of research. We find in

It is said that we normally find that about 50 per cent of Canadian graduate students leave Canada and carry on their research work or their teaching work in the United States. It is necessary for many of them to go to the United States or the United Kingdom to carry on their Ph.D or perhaps their M.A. program, and then having been established in a United States university the opportunities are such that about half of them do not return to Canada.
Then there is the old question of too few scholarships and fellowships for the student in social science who has the aptitude, ability, interest and desire to proceed, but who because of lack of financial backing must forego a career in this field. There are of course grants to students in this category, and I am happy to say that over the recent years they have been increasing. It is significant-I believe this observation lends timeliness to the resolution of the hon. member for Lambton West-that until very recently the funds which were assisting Canadian students in the field of social sciences came from such organizations as the Carnegie Foundation, the Guggenheim Trust, the Ford Foundation, the Rockefeller Foundation, the Nuffield Foundation, or from the private generosity of that great benefactor of education, Lord Beaverbrook; in other words, from sources outside this country. In the field of individual contributions to education from those of its citizens who are blessed with this world's goods, Canada lags far behind the United States and the United Kingdom.
In the overall field of assistance to worthy students the figure for Canada is quite significant. It has been estimated-I have the figures here for 1954 and 1955-that in Great Britain 72.9 per cent of all students registered at British universities were in receipt of some kind of scholarship or bursary. In the United States in the same year 55.9 per cent of all university students enrolled in state universities were in receipt of either all or part of their tuition fee, while 20 per cent of those in private universities were receiving assistance. In Canada, for the same year, the figure for all students was estimated at 14 per cent. This refers to a situation which existed some two or three years ago. Since then the improvement has been considerable, though not substantial.
The hon. member for Halton referred to the national research council, that splendid body which was established in Canada under the administration of Sir Robert Borden. In the field of the social sciences there is no such body. The closest we have to it is a private organization, the Canadian Social Science

Proposal to Increase Research Activities Research Council, which in May of this year will come of age and celebrate its twenty-first birthday. This group of dedicated and interested scholars looking over the field 21 years ago was shocked at the state of research into the social sciences of this country.

They found, 21 years ago that at the undergraduate level geography was taught in only four of the universities, anthropology in fewer still; they found that statistics, sociology and other social sciences did not appear in the curricula of several of the leading universities, and that when they did appear they received scant attention. This Canadian Social Science Research Council discovered that at post graduate level 21 years ago there were 12 scholarships or fellowships offered in the social sciences and 14 in the humanities as compared with 96 in the natural sciences. In its first report, the committee observed:
Considering post graduate scholarships in Canada one is apt to wonder whether they are as much a recognition of scholarship in itself as they are a means of helping along those who have chosen practical careers-studies that are expected to yield a dollars-and-cents return. This emphasis is probably to be expected in a country where so much attention can still be devoted to undeveloped resources, but experience of the 1930's has been such as to make us wonder whether, even from the purely practical point of view, there ought not to be more encouragement given to the study of the social and economic mechanism that enables the resources to be used.
In this connection it is encouraging to report that in the 21 years of this research council's activities much has been accomplished, and that just before the creation of the Canada Council it was possible for it to distribute annually some $150,000 to worthy Canadian institutions of learning and to ambitious and deserving students in Canada.
I feel that if such a committee as is now suggested could be established, it could bring to itself no more valuable and no more highly informed witness than Dr. John Robbins who for 20 years has been secretary of the Canadian social science research council. I am confident that no man in Canada is so familiar with or so deeply concerned about the problems involved in this aspect of research as he is. The Canadian social science research council is still performing a very important role, in that with regard to certain grants made by the Canada Council it is the selecting body. In addition to assisting scholars, the council has also assisted publications, and there is no field of journalism in Canada in which there is greater difficulty in maintaining a situation of solvency than that facing

the learned publications which a mature society must require. In this instance I should be remiss if I did not say that the establishment of the Canada Council was one of the greatest moves in the direction of improving research, especially in the field of the social sciences and the humanities. That was a wonderful step forward and something which I applauded most heartily. As I have seen it function, I congratulate still further those who sponsored this magnificent development.
But though the Canada Council is a mark of national initiative in this field of research, I think still further initiative should be shown on the national level and therefore it is altogether appropriate that we should be discussing the resolution now before us. I think that we in Canada can offer inducements of a tangible kind to stimulate research into many untouched and uncharted areas. They say a country becomes mature when it begins to become aware of its past and take an interest therein. I used the expression "uncharted," and I used it advisedly because in so many areas of Canada's growth and development we find great vacuums so far as research and study are concerned. We have a great dearth of secondary material in the field of history alone. For instance, in Canada we have now, happily, one fine modern work on the great statesman, Sir John A. Macdonald. But why should we not have a dozen? We might compare the situation with that in the United States where the whole field of historical study has become so vast that the volumes on Lincoln alone would establish a very substantial library. There are many figures in the Canadian past which deserve the attention of Canadian scholars. We need our great statesmen assessed by those who were not their contemporary admirers or detractors, though there is an important role for contemporary scholarship as well. There are many other figures, besides prime ministers, whose contributions to the country should certainly be recorded. One could think of many such men. Joseph Howe might be one. Sir Clifford Sifton could be another and I should personally like to see something written about Sir Sam Hughes.
There are other subjects besides history. Canadian scholarship might direct itself to ecology. We are in the midst of a vast change in our urban-rural relationships, yet most Canadian students study sociology today from texts which were written by United States authors about United States conditions. About parliament itself, about political parties, about the whole process of our political institutions, there is much yet to be done, and the inducement and the encouragement of research in this field alone would I think present a very

worth-while challenge and opportunity to the kind of committee we envisage in this resolution.

In February I had the pleasure of attending the opening of a new forest products laboratory in Vancouver. It was a credit to the government. So far we have not been able to use it successfully in the making of pulp and paper because of certain chemical aspects of the wood and the chemical effect on the digesters in the pulp and paper plants. Yet if we are going to derive the most from our forests we must find a use for this low grade cedar product, particularly if we are to continue to maintain our pulp and paper and lumber production on the coast.
We also heard in that committee from a very eminent British Columbia forester, Mr. Ian Mahood, who came here to appear before the committee. He emphasized the need for research in the field of silviculture. He pointed out that one of the greatest problems in British Columbia was to maintain a rapidly producing forest with high productivity in close proximity to the existing plants and developed roads. He pointed out that some countries in the world are making great progress in this particular field. He spoke about the recommendations of the late Mr. Gordon Sloan who acted as a commissioner to investigate the forest problems in British Columbia. He recommended the lumping of research by all agencies, government, industry and university. He also spoke about the necessity of studies of tree seed production and collection, the development of strains


of trees best suited to the geographical climate and soil condition, the suitability of species to site and many other things that would assist in the rapid growing of our forest in close proximity to existing plants and road developments in order that we may maintain a competitive position in the world markets for forest products.
I think most of us are fairly well aware of what the forest industry means to British Columbia and to Canada. Taking the overall picture, it means something in the neighbourhood of $2,400 million a year in production and I believe it means over $1,500 million a year in total exports. This is an industry to which research is vital. The government has not been too generous in the field of forest research, particularly in the field of silviculture. I do not begrudge the money spent on research involving other products but when one compares the expenditures one finds that in the case of rubber $4,307,000 was spent in 1957 and $1,200,000 odd in the case of textiles. I do not say that these amounts are too high by any means-probably they are not sufficient-but the money that has been allocated for forest research is far too meagre for an industry on which the province of British Columbia depends for the greatest part of its livelihood and the whole of Canada depends for a great part of its livelihood.
