Mr. Speaker, when I enter this building through the main doors I am sometimes stopped by the use of the adjectival word "wholesome" in the inscription carved above the main entranceway:
The wholesome sea is at her gates, her gates both east and west.
One would suppose that one would read the words "cruel sea" or perhaps, with poet Dick Diespecker of Vancouver, the "furious sea", or perhaps the "menacing sea". But no, the inscription is, "the wholesome sea is at her gates, her gates both east and west."
I have waited for this debate to speak for a few minutes on the subject of research into the sea, the sea around us, the cruel sea, the mysterious, menacing sea. It could be made a wholesome sea for when we come, as I hope we will, to establish a committee I would hope that in due course that committee would cause to be brought before it persons of expert knowledge who would help it to investigate the development of the sea for future generations as a source

of chemicals and minerals far more abounding than those in our constituencies in the land base areas of Canada.
There is far more food in the sea than there is on the land. The sea is the mother of us all. The sea is the master of our planet. The land is its slave. Three-quarters of the surface of our cooling cosmos is inhabited by the sea. The sea at its greatest depth far exceeds the height of the highest mountain. Briefly, because I come from a coastal riding, because I am a man who lives on the shore of the sea, it seemed to me that I might enliven this debate on research for a few moments by saying a few words about research into the sea and by holding out some idea of what a committee of parliament might bring before it for further examination.
Most of the research into the sea that we have done in Canada has been provoked by the necessities of our military position. At the commencement of the second world war the Royal Canadian Navy had no scientific establishment and was doing no research into the sea. The national research council, largely through the devotion of two of its senior officers, had kept alive a study of acoustics. One of these, Dr. Field, a former student of Dr. Boyle, both from the national research council, established an acoustics department of the national research council in 1930 and at the start of the war what we knew of underwater sound transmission came largely from this study of acoustics and from information made available to Canadians by research teams of the royal navy.
We should remember when we come into this house to discuss defence that it has been the fashion this session to discuss air interception. This inevitably gives rise to a discussion of the circumstances and particulars surrounding the CF-105. This discussion has no particular bearing on another peril, however, which some people consider to be even greater than the peril of air attack. I refer to the peril that lies under the mysterious sea, the peril of submarine attack. We now have truly submersible craft, craft which can journey through the Arctic ocean at the height of the winter season. This was proven by the most recent voyage of the U.S.S. Skate. The feasibility of this undertaking had already been established, that is the possibility of traversing the Arctic under the ice, but last month the U.S.S. Skate established that it could be done during the worst meteorological time in the Arctic.
These submersibles which may some day be turned against us, and for a defence against which we require all the research talent and energy we can bring together, are now capable of long endurance at high speeds

We must remember that in the single month of January, 1940, 100,000 tons of allied shipping were lost to magnetic mines. At that time the German navy had 45 operational submarines. Today the Soviet union has over 600 at sea, any one of which has more striking power and capacity to destroy North America than any German submarine.
In 1940, following that terrible month of January, two professors from Dalhousie university in Halifax were asked by the Royal Canadian Navy to commence research into the perils of the sea. Doctors G. H. Henderson and J. H. L. Johnstone were asked to commence inquiries into defensive measures Which could be taken to protect allied shipping against the perils of the magnetic mine. Dr. Henderson visited London. I do not know that this story has ever been fully told. Sufficient time has now elapsed that interest can be assuaged without national security being in any way imperilled. Dr. Henderson went to the United Kingdom. It was, perhaps, logical that Halifax should have been chosen as the place upon which to base this research.
Back in the terrible days of the war Halifax and its sister city of Saint John were indispensable to this nation. Alas, sometimes we are subsequently forgotten, but thereby hangeth another tale. Dr. Henderson returned and visited Dean Mackenzie at the national research council. A small amount of money and a small number of personnel were made available. During the war, in my harbour, 3,800 allied vessels carrying the produce of every one of our constituencies, carrying the sinews of war, underwent degaussing at a range established in Bedford basin adjoining Halifax harbour.
It is typical of military weapons that as fast as you find defensive measures against them they are superseded by new types of equipment or new techniques of use. At the end of the war a separate naval research establishment was created. I refer to the laboratory of the defence research board which has its headquarters at Dartmouth across the harbour from Halifax. Here is concentrated, in conjunction with applied research of the Department of Fisheries oceanographic station at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, almost all the substance and total of Canadian research into our greatest physical asset, the wholesome sea which is at our gates. This research is largely concentrated in these two locations. Here, since the war; here, since the creation of separate physical facilities in 1952, in the town of Dartmouth,

It is typical of most scientists that they are interested, a priori, in the achievement of their scientific research, not in its application. It is typical also of the naval scientists that they are indeed the most silent members of the silent service. Some of the results of this research, which are possible of limited civilian application, would be of incalculable benefit to Canadians. The naval research establishment in Dartmouth is presently preoccupied mostly with work of a highly secret nature, classified security work having to do with the detection of submarines, the increase of fire control mechanisms and the improvement of ordnance as a defence and as a direct countermeasure against submarines.
However, in addition to this classified work, the story of which will have to wait perhaps for some future generations, there has been some other work done. It is this type of work which I would hope that a research committee would inquire into and expand, if possible. The naval research establishment at Dartmouth has conducted continuing experiments with a hydrofoil craft. It is interesting to tell, and I think for the first time publicly, that the modern hydrofoil craft now visible in Halifax harbour under trial actually originated with a request of the then general officer commanding the Pacific region, now the distinguished Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes), who asked during the late war that the Suffield experimental station produce a portable smokescreen device to be used in amphibious assaults. As a result of this request research was conducted which revived experiments first conducted in 1907 by Alexander Graham Bell, John A. D. McCurdy and Casey Baldwin at Bras d'Or in Nova Scotia. These were the three men who had, in fact, created the Silver Dart, the first heavier than air craft to be flown in Canada and who also created the first hydrofoil craft. It is interesting that as a result of all our research we have come back, after several years, to their basic prototype. This hydrofoil craft is the forerunner of a new ship design because the research establishes that the hydrofoil principle can now be adapted to other vessels.
The naval research establishment at Dartmouth has also been engaged in research into scale formation on the coils of freshwater evaporators used by our ships at sea. We as Canadians have an enormous capital investment in naval ships. Yet if we had no fresh water aboard them, men could not stay at sea for indefinite periods. In this regard,


it is interesting to note that our sister parliamentary group, namely the United States congress, has voted $10 million for advanced research in that country into the conversion of salt water into fresh water. The United States' secretary of the interior, Mr. Seaton, early last month announced that that research in the United States had advanced to such a degree that it was now possible to procure fresh water from salt water at a cost of one dollar per thousand gallons. This compares with a present cost of fresh water to domestic households in the city of Ottawa of approximately twenty cents per one thousand gallons. I mention this matter lest any hon. member from an inland constituency think that the result of research into the sea would have no direct bearing upon his constituency. My farm member friends across the floor of the house must surely be interested in any venture which can produce fresh water from salt water at a reasonable economic cost. If the cost can be further reduced the impact upon the world's food production would be inmeasurable.
The naval research establishment at Dartmouth has also done pioneering research into marine paints to prevent or resist corrosion and rusting, particularly below the water line. The naval research establishment is also examining and researching the use of other alternative materials for ship construction. Finally, in this symbolic recital of this incalculable work, may I say that the naval research establishment is engaged, in conjunction with the fisheries research stations, in basic research into oceanography. Here we come face to face with the future of our world, for the sea, the wholesome sea, contains more minerals than does the land area, more chemicals and more food life. Yet in today's atomic age it is a little saddening to reflect that we know more about the moon than we know about our own sea.
At the naval research establishment in Dartmouth even as I speak experiments are being conducted into such basic research information as thermal gradients and salinity gradients off the Nova Scotia coast which is one presenting peculiar problems for oceanographic research for not only does the temperature of the water change in location and as it deepens, but it also changes with the seasons.
I cannot overemphasize to my fellow members of all parties in the house, the absolute indispensability to the welfare of all the people in all the parts of Canada who sent us here of the research which is conducted today, by chance in my constituency, into the nature of sound transmission in the sea. It is now theoretically possible for a submarine to lie under a layer of water where there

is a sudden change in temperature or even in salinity and there be relatively unreachable by detection gear. It is possible that this research into the sea will be the means whereby, in conjunction with other defence mechanisms, we shall buy our survival in an atomic age. But I would hold out the hope-as I know would other hon. members [DOT]-that this research into a special field, namely research into the sea, would some day be useful to us not in protecting ourselves against death from nuclear-headed, underwater-launched missiles but that it would be useful to us in transmitting to all the world's peoples the hope that at long last we shall be able to gather in the bounty of the sea and that when we enter this building we shall not ceaselessly wonder about the adjectival use of the word in the inscription over the main door:
The wholesome sea is at her gates, her gates both east and west.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been said that 40 years of scientific research on a national scale or basis has made it possible for Canada to keep pace with the exploitations of its own vast resources as well as with the accelerated economic development noticeable in all parts of the world. This statement is found in a recent edition of the Canada Year Book. We may or may not agree with this statement. It is clear that the great research in the past has brought great benefit to our country. In listening to the debate this afternoon we have learned that there are many fields in which research is still necessary. For that reason I think the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) is to be congratulated for having brought this motion before us in order to give us the opportunity of reasoning with the government with a view to having it set up the committee that he has suggested.
In going over the past we have seen that as a result of the first world war the government at that time set up the national research council. Then in 1924, as a result of experience, it was reorganized. This council has given leadership in many fields of research and has provided grants and scholarships to encourage research. Because of the experiences of the second world war, the defence research board was established in order to give leadership in research necessary for the defence of Canada. We have already proved the necessity of research and the benefits of it. Today we are considering the advisability of reviewing our efforts in the field of research.
I therefore raise two fundamental questions in respect to this. Should we not now consider our capacity to extend such research? Have we sufficient facilities to train
Proposal to Increase Research Activities the personnel necessary to develop such research? Does our educational system provide the opportunity and the incentive which will produce the research personnel necessary for the work that is to be carried out? Secondly, to what extent should we endeavour to develop the full intellectual potential in our human resources? The answer to these questions would involve research in numerous fields and problems related to education, such as the teaching and training of our gifted children, the use of television in our educational system, the teaching and training of our handicapped children, the curriculum requirements for our present society, and the financing of education.
The federal government has recognized the need of assistance and the importance of research and education, and is giving increasing assistance. The provincial governments have recognized the need and importance and are giving it increased assistance also. Universities have been expanding research facilities, and they have been assisted by government and private grants. Some local boards have recognized the importance of research, such as the Toronto board of education, which has set up a research department and is providing space for this department in its new administrative building. I submit that this house has ample proof of the need to set up a committee to study the needs in the field of research, and I would like to suggest that when this committee is set up and meets it should study the need of research in the field of education.
To support this view I quote from the brief to the federal government from the Canadian teachers' federation presented in 1958. On page 9 of that brief they state as follows:
Research is an important aspect of improvement of education. In Canada there is no co-ordinated program of educational research. While the work done has been creditable, it has suffered from want of financial support except in the case of a few projects financed by grants from foundations, mostly in the United States.
The Canadian teachers' federation for the past five years has maintained a research division which costs approximately a quarter of its annual budget. The education division of the dominion bureau of statistics renders a valuable service in the provision of statistical research but it is greatly hampered by lack of staff. A few of the faculties of education in Canadian universities are conducting some research. However, all of these add up to a very inadequate program if Canada is to remain abreast of some other countries and in line with changing conditions in our social, economic, and scientific advances.
The federation recommends that the federal government give consideration to providing at least some of the financial support necessary to establish and maintain a central bureau of educational research. Such a bureau could co-ordinate work now being done throughout Canada, stimulate

and conduct new research and generally render a service to this aspect of the improvement of education.
I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that if we are going to consider the research problems into our physical assets we cannot overlook the need of the skilled researchers to carry out this work. We must give encouragement and assistance to the educational groups throughout this country to provide the opportunities and facilities to train research workers, and for that reason I think it is necessary that the federal government study in any project such as this the implications which it would have in the educational field. I sometimes wonder what is the percentage of the personnel involved in the research which is being done which have been trained in our own universities or school system. I also point out that in the field of research itself education is a very fertile ground in which this research should be carried out, and I hope that in the consideration of a committee which may be set up there is not overlooked the need of research in education.

Mr. Speaker, like others who have spoken on this resolution, my first words must be words of congratulation to the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy), who has proposed this resolution and who has put forward his case in support of it so ably in this house today and on previous occasions. In preparing to speak on this matter I did some research in Hansard, and I found that the past contributions of the hon. member for Lambton West and of many of his colleagues who were then sitting in opposition were most informative. I would suggest that if anything is left out in today's debate it would very likely be included in past debates on this matter in this house. In particular I would refer hon. members to a speech made by the hon. member for Lambton West on May 11, 1954. This speech may be found in volume 5 of the revised Hansard for the 195354 session at page 4630. There he suggests that in dealing with this topic we ask ourselves several questions, and I would suggest to the house that those questions which are found on that page are just as applicable today as they were at that time. I will not repeat those questions as they are somewhat lengthy and I am sure there are others who would like to speak on this matter. I therefore merely refer the members of this house to those questions which may be found in Hansard.
There are a great many aspects of research that could be dealt with, and it is difficult for any hon. member to touch upon them all. We have heard from various quarters today


and we have heard various aspects of research discussed very fully and ably. To my mind research is essential for our survival both from a military and an economic point of view. We are all well aware, I am sure, of the tremendous advances which have been made in soviet Russia in the field of research and in the field of education. They have made advances in the field of military weapons, and these advances are all quite well known to us in this house. They have made advances in industry, in agriculture and in various other fields, and these strides have enabled them to compete for and obtain world markets from which they were previously excluded.
In order to discuss the present situation in Canada I should like for a moment to refer to the situation which existed in this country in 1938-39. I must apologize for the figures to which I will refer, inasmuch as they are not completely accurate figures, and this is for the simple reason that it is very difficult to obtain accurate figures in terms of dollars and cents when one is discussing this subject. However, I am sure that even though these figures may not be completely reliable they will serve to illustrate the situation which existed at that time. In 1938-39 the amount spent by the Canadian government on research was between 40 cents and 50 cents reckoned on a per capita basis. This figure applied not only to Canada but also to the United States and to the United Kingdom. In comparison, the expenditure on a per capita basis by industry in Canada during the same period was approximately 20 cents, and in Britain it ranged between 30 cents and 50 cents. In the United States, on the other hand, the surprising amount of $1.70 per head of the population was being spent by private industry. Today in Canada, as nearly as I can find from the material I have accumulated, the government is spending approximately $1 on research, on a per capita basis, and private industry is spending $1.35. These figures, though they may not be accurate, as I have explained, are somewhat below the figure which the United States was spending in 1938-39, and for that reason I ask the question: is Canadian industry doing all it can in the field of research? Regardless of what they are spending, are they realizing their total potential? I think this is one aspect of the subject which the committee proposed in this motion might study in detail. Having studied it, the committee would be in position to recommend to the government how industry could be encouraged to spend more on research. It would also be in a position to offer guidance to industry in developing its products and competing for markets.

I think many of us at the present time see far too many situations where parts of industry-certain aspects of industry-have become wholly dependent on government contracts. One cannot help but ask the question: are such companies doing anything for themselves. One cannot, of course, apply this criticism to every industry in this country, but I think there are certain industries which feel that there is a gold mine underneath the centre block and that all they need to do is raise enough fuss and they will get contracts. Such firms are completely disregarding one of their responsibilities as free enterprise companies in a free enterprise nation, and that is basic research-to come up with a product and then to sell it.
I wonder if I might call it six o'clock?

Today we have the atomic bomb and the hydrogen bomb, and much is being done in this country in promoting the development of atomic energy for peaceful uses; but I do not think we should conclude that the atomic bomb and the hydrogen bomb are the ultimate so far as weapons of warfare are concerned. Nonetheless, that does not derogate from the fact that we on this side of the house think that in essence the resolution is a good one.
In fact, I think that the house knows full well the attitude and conduct of the former administration with reference to research. I have no intention of recalling what that is. If I felt that I would not be taking up the time of the house I would go into them in greater detail. However, as one member has stated already, I believe that this is a matter which should be disposed of as quickly as possible and I have no intention of delaying the passage of the resolution.
I did rise, however, with one other purpose in mind, to put on Hansard the attitude of the Liberal party with reference to this matter. It has already been discussed in the house but not under this heading and I thought I should like to read at this time


the statement of policy approved by the party so far as research is concerned. It is in these words:
We propose to establish a national science commission to co-ordinate, promote and sponsor scientific development and research in Canada. The purpose would be to ensure, through appropriate financial assistance and the effective use of our resources, an adequate program of basic and applied scientific research through the national research council, the defence research board and other government agencies, together with industry and the universities.
I believe that most other hon. members who have spoken on the resolution have touched upon the various aspects of this Liberal party program. Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased this evening to support the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy). In his resolution he suggests a special committee, representative of all parties to examine, to promote and accelerate activities in the field of research. In my view no person in the house is better qualified to propose such a resolution than the hon. member for Lambton West, for he represents an area which has become known as the chemical valley of Canada and the products manufactured in this valley are widely distributed and widely known all over the world. I am sure that since he first became a member of the house in 1945 he has seen at each session the growing need for a much greater acceleration in the field of research. I wish to congratulate him for bringing this most important subject before the house for discussion not only on this occasion but during other sessions.
The hon. member for Lambton West, speaking on the subject of research on May

11, 1954, proposed a series of questions and I wish to quote a few of them at this time. As found at page 4630 of Hansard his questions were as follows:
1.	Are we doing enough in the way of research in this country, in view of the vast and varied natural resources now known to exist in commercial quantities in Canada?
2.	Are our universities in a position to continue to provide the trained scientific minds and undertake the fundamental research necessary to assure the continued development and productive expansion of this country?
3.	Would accelerated efforts in the field of industrial research, resulting in new products, new uses for old products, improved techniques that lower production costs, enhance or help us, an exporting nation is ever-increasingly competitive world markets?
4.	Are our present fiscal policies, in relation to research expenditures, adequate to induce private industry to undertake the amount of research that should be undertaken other than by government agencies, if we are to continue to enjoy a high level of capital investment so essential to high employment and general prosperity in this country?
5.	Does the government do enough in the way of agricultural, medical and other research, in fields where this can best be accomplished by the state in the common interest of all its citizens?
6.	How does the degree and extent of research in this country compare with comparable efforts in the United States, the United Kingdom and other countries with whom our primary and secondary producers must complete in export markets?
I feel that these questions, Mr. Speaker, were important in 1954, almost five years ago, and are just as important and probably more so today than they were at that time. Tonight I wish to discuss one phase of a research program and that is in the field of agriculture. Research in agriculture has been concerned largely with practical problems and in this regard contributes greatly to the industry. But viewed as a specific program it means finding wider outlets for agricultural products; it means finding new uses in a wider field for edible and inedible agricultural products, for as we continue to expand in industry a greater need arises for raw materials. Much of this raw material can come from our agricultural products.
I wish to give credit to the tremendous contribution our agricultural scientists have made in the field of agriculture in the past. If it had not been for the contribution of a great scientist, Dr. Saunders, we would not have had Marquis wheat. Later, when rust threatened the varieties of wheat grown in western Canada, research again came to the rescue and a new variety was introduced that was fairly immune to the rust spores. What would be the position of our agricultural producers today if we did not have scientific agricultural research to improve and produce new varieties of cereal grains?

Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to take this opportunity, like previous speakers, to offer my most sincere congratulations to the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) upon his introduction to the House of Commons today of a most pressing and timely subject which certainly merits the interest and general discussion of the members of this house. Just a few minutes ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Smith) drew our atttention to the fact that this problem is one which must be faced not only by governments, be they federal, provincial or municipal, but by all segments our society; -government, industry, community associations and labour.

Proposal to Increase Research Activities
I am more than pleased, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Lambton West, at the outset of his remarks, decided to offer a definition of the word "research". Referring to the Oxford dictionary he gave us a classical definition of exactly what the word "research" means. I say this is most important, Mr. Speaker, because in a very few minutes I want to point out that we are dealing with a subject which is part and parcel of a wider, though not necessarily more significant, subject. I refer to the delicate question of dominion-provincial relations.
If you would permit me to digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, I should like to relate to this house an incident which occurred a few years ago. At that time I had the privilege of watching a number of sittings of the United States congress. They were dealing with a bill which was essentially a bill related to education but which touched upon many aspects of research. While we must admit that the United States federal constitution is not exactly like that of the federal constitution which governs the Dominion of Canada, one had to admit that congress was experiencing a certain amount of difficulty in securing the passage of this educational or research bill. The reason was that, not unlike the provinces of Canada, the states of the United States of America guarded most jealously their rights over education. Speaker after speaker, therefore, had to get up and demonstrate that this was extraordinary legislation they were attempting to pass, and that certainly it was being passed because of the emergency conditions which, to a certain degree, did exist in relation to research and education. This is one question we can ask ourselves today in relation to domestic and world events. Do emergency conditions exist, not in the definite and dogmatic sense of the word "emergency", but do emergency conditions exist in relation to this problem?
As I said before, the problem of research which has been discussed today must not be necessarily mixed up with the problem of education per se, although it is readily admitted that both research and education are most definitely interrelated. I think that although we as federal legislators are not keen to get up in this house and discuss in their entirety simple matters which fall essentially within the provincial domain, we must be realistic in tackling any question of research in this federal house. We must be realistic and admit that this problem is only going to be solved with harmonious dominion-provincial relations. It is upon this basis that I should like to make a few brief, pertinent remarks.
I do not want to enter the field of partisan politics at the moment, but it is a fact that
[Mr. Grafftey.l
when this administration assumed office dominion-provincial relations were not good. I think it is fair to say that past Liberal ministers of finance-certainly, it seemed that way to many of us who were residents of the province of Quebec-did not even care to recognize that there was such a thing as a problem existing in connection with tax matters. Since the present administration has come to power the whole atmosphere has begun to change. Time and time again we can see that we have at least recognized the problems and we are going to try to work them out under harmonious and friendly conditions.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to revert to my initial remarks. I should like to say that it was extremely important that the mover of this motion attempted to give us a very reasonable definition of the word "research".
Many provincial leaders in the province of Quebec naturally have worries when they see a motion of this type in relation to research. Naturally they have worries as to what we think research actually means. Let us consider, for example, the many French-speaking classical colleges and schools in the province of Quebec. What will be defined as research or as aid to research in relation to these institutions? I think it is a well known fact-and it might as well be spoken about and aired frankly in this house-that under the terms of the British North America Act the provincial authorities in the province which I represent guard most jealously provincial rights over education. But that fact should not make us pessimistic in dealing with this most worthy resolution. It should only make us more aware of the absolute necessity for defining the word "research".
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks on the problem of research in relation to some statements made by an illustrious Canadian, a great Christian, a humanitarian, a great scientist, neurosurgeon and neurologist and now in his later years a great author. I refer to Doctor Wilder Pen-field, O.M., director of the Montreal neurological institute. I think that we as Canadians should be proud to count him amongst our most illustrious citizens.
I have made a few brief notes here, Mr. Speaker, on some remarks made recently by Doctor Penfield on education and research at the twenty-third annual meeting of the Montreal neurological institute on May 14, 1958. While his report has particular application to the above-mentioned institute, many of his remarks have broad significance in relation to the field of research. As he takes a look at research in Canada today, especially higher

research, he feels that the best educated and trained nation is the strongest and happiest and best able to defend itself and to realize its own potential. The problem of the institute is the problem of many similar institutions in the field of higher education and research. They teach graduate students. They are carefully selected scholars and expert technicians prepared to take up their life's work. Like Doctor Penfield did, they are laying plans. Some will found university or hospital units of their own. Undoubtedly they will secure research grants from some foundation, government or patient.
Doctor Penfield feels that research institutions like nations must take a long view. Mr. Speaker, I listened with very great pleasure this afternoon to the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) when he proposed this resolution which has to do with research. I also was very happy to hear all hon. members who this afternoon made suggestions and spoke of the significance of research in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, research is at the root of all progress in any country. In that field, we should not leave too much to luck or chance. Developments must be prepared and the march of science must be guided into proper channels. Research should not be restricted to the scientific field but should apply to all areas likely to improve the lot of man. In a country like ours, at the crossroads of two ages and two worlds, it is important to adjust research first to modern conditions and then to the geographical pattern.
Modern conditions, for instance, tend to promote research in the great Canadian Northland, and to intensify it in that area so as to discover the mineral wealth of our soil, like oil, gold or other resources. In the geographic field, research must be activated in that direction so as to improve and develop means of communication throughout the country as they are essential to the uniform development of all parts of a country.
Mr. Speaker, in Canada research can be as vast as the country itself, but must be proceeded with in the same way as was the case for our other natural resources. Canada to date has produced excellent research workers to whom we owe the advance of our country and who have achieved an enviable reputation among the world's scientists.
This afternoon, we in this house had the pleasure to hear the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Best), and hon. members were immediately reminded of the famous development we owe to those two great Canadians, Dr. Best and Dr. Banting, the discoverers of insulin.
Many of our research workers have become prominent in all fields of science. In the field of agriculture, need I mention the famous Marquis wheat, which is a Canadian development? That wheat continues to make Canada better known throughout the world.
Need I refer to such prominent research workers as the late brother Marie Victorin, a great scientist, who had the things of
[Mr. Grafftey.l

nature at heart but always remained in the field of science. He specialized in the field of plants: botany.
Need I mention Professor Lower, an historian of great renown, or Canon Groulx, a great research worker whose many historical accounts can be found today in all Canadian libraries?
For the moment research in Canada must be placed in its natural setting. Research is being made in the field of science, of pure and applied science. In the field of pure science need I mention the wonderful work accomplished by the National Research Council whose fame is well established throughout the world? In the field of applied science, we have in Chalk River an atomic energy laboratory and it is worthy of note that the research work being carried out there is solely directed to peaceful uses. Canada may not be as advanced in the field of research, as other and more prosperous countries of the world, for instance, the United States who have monopolized the best brains in the world. In fact, Berkeley University, in California, has seven Nobel prize winners among its teaching staff.
Canada is forging ahead in agricultural research, in industrial and scientific research of all kinds, and it can be said that our country, proportionately speaking, considering its population and its financial means, is second to none in the field of research.

Mr. Speaker, it is also most important that our research centres obtain the funds they need for medical research; they should be given the necessary funds to step up research in the fields of heart disease and cancer. When a war breaks out, millions of dollars are found for armaments. Today, millions of dollars should be made available to research laboratories to enable them to step up their work against cancer, because we all know that no cure has yet been found for cancer of the blood. Canada has many research laboratories. Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to remind you of the importance of the University of Montreal's institute of microbiology, directed by an outstanding professor, Dr. Frappier. This laboratory enjoys a worldwide reputation; it is a credit not only to the province of Quebec but to the country as a whole.
In the industrial field, many research projects are being carried out. Companies make millions of dollars available to their technologists in order to further scientific progress. Do I have to mention to you that, in the province of Quebec, the city of St. Hyacinthe has a school of research on textiles which is held in high repute even beyond the province of Quebec?
The paper-making school in Three Rivers has a miniature paper mill which is the most

Research in refining and petroleum must also be carried out on a larger scale.
Scientists must be encouraged to do research work, to intensify their research, for instance in the field of humanities, history, folklore and literature.
In the field of history, need I recall the name of Mr. Jean Bruchesi, recently appointed Canadian ambassador abroad? It is a recognized fact that he has done much research work in the field of history.

Many professional journalists also do research work.
Mr. Speaker, we have many scientists, but unfortunately, we may not have enough of them in the field of philosophy and sociology.
In what manner can we promote research? Provincial governments should be encouraged to grant scholarships to students. The Canadian government should also be encouraged to increase the number of scholarships granted for research only or for the exchange of students between countries. Funds should be voted to improve the laboratories, to encourage young people to work in earnest. Finally the necessary grant should be made to research institutions.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the national research council be made to act as co-ordinator of research in Canada. Research knows no boundaries.
Perhaps one of the best means of simplifying research would be to adopt the metric system. In the light of studies that have been made, there is no doubt that the adoption of the metric system would help simplify research. Mr. Speaker, I am very glad of the oppor-

tunity that the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) has given to me by putting forth such a resolution because it enables me sincerely to express some of my views, especially in the field of scientific research. I feel, sir, that the criticism that we see from time to time in the newspapers and hear from people across the country to some extent as to the lopsided representation in parliament is justified. By that I mean we have the talking groups of lawyers, school teachers, labour leaders and so forth, as opposed to perhaps the working people, those who are actually doing things, such as the scientists.
Since the beginning of this session I have listened to some observations made on perhaps one of the most outstanding things that affects us world-wide, namely the international geophysical year, which was conceived by scientists down in the United States in April, 1950, and which finally came into existence and ran for a period of 18 months from July 31, 1957, to December 31, 1958. During this time some 30,000 scientists and technicians from some 66 nations took part in a crash program of data collecting to enable us to know a little bit more about this world. I feel, as one of the members of the talking class, being a lawyer, that I am in a rather inadequate position to put forth perhaps the point of view of the scientists; but I feel nevertheless that it is one of the inadequacies of parliament that we have no scientific representation in this group who is able to speak on such an important and noteworthy resolution. Therefore, I have allotted the task to myself with a certain amount of temerity.
The most important aspect of research in the international geophysical year which interested me was the matter of space research. This was accomplished through several means; first, the sounding rockets; second, the earth satellites; and, third, what they call deep-space vehicles. In the first category of the sounding rockets, some several hundred rockets were launched from the United States, the Soviet union, Britain and Japan. In the second category of earth satellites, during the international geophysical year some four were launched from the United States and three from the Soviet union. During this same international geophysical year the only deep-space vehicle launched was launched by the United States, namely the Pioneer, which went up to a distance of some 80,000 miles.
Hon. members may ask what were some of the results that we have obtained so far from
Proposal to Increase Research Activities the international geophysical year? First, and perhaps the most important in the matter of space research, was the discovery of the Van Allen radiation layer. This is an area of very intense radiation extending from some 600 miles to some 21,500 miles above the earth. Apparently this particular radiation layer is not so dense at the poles. This is of interest to the space research people in the sense that it may pose further difficulties when man eventually travels out into space.
One of the other things which has come out of the international geophysical year so far and which is of interest to us is in contrast with what was thought in 1492 at the time of Christopher Columbus. People laughed when Christopher thought that the earth was round. We have had a vision since 1492 of a round earth. Yet the scientists taking part in the international geophysical year have said that the picture they have now is of a pear-shaped earth, one that is flattened at the poles and somewhat pear-shaped toward the South American region. One problem which has been raised by the activities of the international geophysical year and which would benefit from interest on the part of such groups as ourselves is the question of the distance between the Atlantic and the Pacific because even in this modern age the exact distance is not known. True, it may only be a matter of one or two miles that is involved but even though we are in a scientific era it still is not known.
Another matter of interest is the question of the effect of the tidal waves actually involved in the earth. The earth too has tidal waves exactly the same as water. In fact, the scientists say that places like Hawaii rise and fall several inches in the course of one day. It is hoped that the research of the international geophysical year will give more definite information regarding this particular matter.
I think also of the question of space rockets and space research. As parliamentarians I think we should be very much interested. However, since the beginning of this session I do not believe we have had anything but oblique reference to the international geophysical year and its accomplishments. The postmaster general of the United States of America is interested in transporting mail by rockets. I wonder whether the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) of Canada has given any consideration to the matter or is similarly

Proposal to Increase Research Activities interested. Perhaps that is a slightly facetious reference but we are actually in the space era and recognition is being given to such possibilities.
The resolution of the hon. member for Lambton West covers the providing of inducements to promote and accelerate activities in the field of research. So far as scientific research is concerned, I think that one of the first things that we as members of parliament must do is to show some interest in the subject. In my opinion such a committee could give consideration to the establishment of a parliamentary space committee to study this matter and receive reports from scientists as to what is actually going on in other parts of the world with regard to space and other scientific research. I feel that this matter should be of interest and I think that in the very near future we will see the establishment of a ministry of space. With our rather simple legal principles regarding space ownership permeating down to the centre of the earth and somewhere into the upper regions, it will become very important to Canada to have a clear understanding of what control it can and will exert with regard to outer space.
I realize that a small country like Canada does not have the money to enter into space research to the same degree as the Soviet union, Great Britain and the United States but nevertheless I believe that as members of parliament we should show some leadership and take an interest in space research. I believe that the United States has such a government committee and if we had a space committee there could be liaison with their committee. We would then be able to keep in the vanguard of development instead of being still on the ground back in the horse and buggy era while other nations are looking upwards. I believe that the resolution of the hon. member for Lambton West provides an opportunity for Canada to take the necessary scientific leadership.

I was particularly glad to hear this in view of the fact that on March 1, 1956 a similar motion was presented to the house by the parliamentary assistant to the then minister of defence production. The motion at that time read as follows:
That a special committee be appointed to examine into the role of government in the field of non-military research in Canada, including:
(a)	operations in the field of atomic energy.

That the committee be empowered to sit during
the sittings of the house and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the committee and to report from time to time; and that notwithstanding standing order No. 67 the committee shall consist of 20 members.
The arrangements provided for that committee were very similar to the committee the hon. member for Lambton West has in mind but with one important difference. The resolution now before us provides that the committee can call for witnesses and send for documents and papers and goes on to say that the committee should be appointed for the purpose of examining and reporting on the advisability of providing inducements to promote and accelerate activities in the field of research.
The only difference between the two resolutions is that the committee envisaged by the hon. member for Lambton West would have the power to send for experts in the person of professors, scientists, technologists of various kinds, and for documents and papers so that the committee would have concrete information on which to work and would not be working on speculation. However, back in 1956, and I think this is important, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Green) moved an amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Lambton West, to the government motion, that amendment being in these words:
That the motion be amended by inserting after the word "house" in the sixth line thereof the following:
"To send for persons and unclassified papers and records."
It is interesting to note that on that date, March 1, 1956, the members of the government then in power voted against that amendment, the result of the vote being 127 nays and 72 yeas. At that time the three opposition parties, the Progressive Conservatives, the C.C.F. and the Social Credit, all voted in favour of the amendment. It is for this reason that I am very delighted to see that spokesmen for the Liberal party in the house

today have indicated their support of the motion now before us. Apparently they have had a change of heart in the meantime, possibly due to the fact that they now sit across the floor.
I do not wish to take up the time of the house by reiterating what has already been said by many other members, nor to bring before the house questions which I am sure are in the minds of the general public. I refer, of course, to the necessity of basic research being increased in Canada because of the very rapid advancement by what may be considered the potential enemy, namely the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. There has been repeatedly brought to everyone's attention by the press, radio and prominent speakers the extent to which Russia has been able to mobilize her vast resources of men and raw materials, and also her almost machine-like production of scientists, engineers and technologists. I well recall that in 1956, I think it was, I made remarks in this house dealing with this subject. I do not intend to repeat them now. It is nothing short of a miracle the extent to which Russia has been able to emerge from virtually a feudal economy almost 38 years ago into practically the world's leading industrial power. This has been accomplished by encouraging scientists, technologists and basic research. I think we can learn a lesson from that.
It is true that in this country, the United States and other western countries we have developed a very high standard of living. We have done very well. I think there is a growing tendency, because we have done well from a material standpoint, for our people to sit back, rest on their oars and say, "Well, we are there." The fact that somebody else is coming along makes little difference. But, Mr. Speaker, the people of Asia, Africa and those countries newly formed since world war II do not have what they call luxuries and what we consider as daily necessities. They are getting pretty tired of getting along on mere subsistence. They are looking with eager eyes toward countries which will help them and which can produce what they consider to be the luxuries of life and which, at the present time, we consider to be the necessities. The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics is more and more coming into the position of being able to do this. If we continue to permit the U.S.S.R. to give help and provide the materials which they will be able to do in the future, then there is no question but that we will have lost the economic war which is being waged in the world today. We will certainly have lost it in so far as the underdeveloped countries are concerned.

Proposal to Increase Research Activities It is true that we have been very helpful to these countries, but if we were going ahead at the same rate as Russia we might do a great deal more. We would not have the worries we have at the present time.
Now, coming a little closer to home, I would say that this problem of encouraging basic research is certainly of great interest and importance to Canada from a domestic point of view. I know that various members have already mentioned the question of basic research. It has been dealt with by others probably better than I could deal with it. However, I should like to point out three things. If a committee such as the one suggested were set up and had the power to send for experts, to send for reports, to look into the matter as carefully as possible, it is quite likely that three of the major domestic problems in Canada might be on the way to solution, not complete solution, but at least a start made toward the solution of these problems.
There is the problem of seasonal unemployment in Canada which we have because of our climate. There is the problem of the huge surpluses, agricultural and otherwise, that have been built up in this country. There is the problem we have as a result of the loss of our domestic and export markets because of high production costs in Canada. In so far as seasonal unemployment is concerned, I am quite sure that if such a committee as is proposed in this resolution were established, scientists and engineers could be called who might suggest avenues of research in the field of winter construction. It is a well known fact that the great problem of seasonal unemployment in Canada is created by the fact that the building industry cannot carry on work during the winter. I know some progress has been made in this field. Only last winter in my own city I saw a bridge being built which had a plastic dome arrangement over it and work which could not have been done heretofore except in the summer months was being done. This bridge was largely built during the winter months.
Further research along this line would greatly improve the possibility of carrying out construction programs in the winter. This would aid in solving some of the problems we have in connection with seasonal unemployment in the building industry. Needless to say, this would be of great importance to this country and in particular to the people who are employed in the building industry. I know of one or two construction firms who are spending considerable of their own money, in a small way, in an attempt to produce metal frames for these plastic domes. These metal frames are put together like the mechano sets with which the youngsters play.

This is only one example, but it illustrates the type of thing which I have in mind. The results of these projects could aid greatly in ironing out the hills and valleys, as the statisticians call them, in the graph of winter employment in the building industry.
Then, there is the problem which faces the fishing industry in the wintertime because of severe weather. I am quite sure that research into this problem could improve the possibility of conducting fishing operations during the more rigorous winter months. This is the sort of thing that this committee could do which would be of practical help to the Canadian people and to those of us who are busily trying to find methods of solving the seasonal unemployment problem in Canada.
The second thing I have in mind is the huge surpluses we have built up in the various agricultural products. The ones that come to mind, of course, are wheat and dry skim milk powder. No doubt hon. members can think of other things. It is very difficult for various reasons, as all hon. members I am sure are aware, to dispose of these surpluses even on a giveaway basis or at a very low price. I think an effort might be made to find substitute uses for some of these large agricultural surpluses. A scientist friend of mine said that some of his associates were working on the problem of converting some of these agricultural products-I have forgotten which ones but I think wheat was one-into some type of plastic which could be readily used. This would provide a market for some of these agricultural surpluses, and this is another example which illustrates the type of thing that could be investigated by this committee.
Then, of course, there is the very important question of the loss of our domestic and export markets because of the high cost of production in Canada. We all know that Canada faces stiff competition as a result of the low wage levels in Asiatic countries. For example the employees in the plywood industry in Japan receive 20 cents an hour, while in Canada they receive $1.65 per hour. Certainly we in Canada have not the slightest desire to reduce our wage levels. Until such time as the wage levels in these countries catch up to our level, we must find some way of manufacturing in Canada which will enable us to compete with these low wage economies in the east.
There are two ways we can do that. First of all, this committee could look into ways


and means of producing new and better products. This would be one method of competing with these low wage economies. The second and obvious way is to find new and better methods of producing present day products. This, again, would be something that this committee could investigate and thus contribute a great deal to the economy of the country. Of course, we all know that many large firms are already spending a great deal of money, time and effort on research, but I do not think there is anyone in this house who would not agree that our research effort in Canada cannot be greatly improved upon.
If this proposed committee had a chance to call all sorts of experts, look into records and information which is available I am sure it would make a helpful recommendation to the government as to how research could best be improved and increased and what inducements would be necessary. It may not be entirely a matter of money. There may be some other method. However, there must be some way of improving and helping to increase research in Canada generally. In particular, I think this committee could look into the possibility of improving research with respect to those three problems I mentioned, namely seasonal unemployment, the disposal of our huge surplus of agricultural products and the loss of our domestic and export markets owing to the high cost of production in Canada.
I should like to close my remarks at this time because I do not wish to go into details. Those are three broad principles which I think could be looked into carefully by this committee. By doing so I think it could contribute a great deal in helping the government to deal with these three problems which have always been with us.

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying before the other debate developed, I propose to speak on this special research committee more in line with the field of agriculture. I think one should realize just how important research is to this great country of Canada, and one need only think of the great amount of research that was put into the development of the St. Lawrence seaway and what has developed from that research field. Never before in the history of Canada would a research committee be more necessary than it is today, especially in the field of agriculture as mentioned here this afternoon and this evening, due to the large amount of surplus agricultural products in Canada. One only need think of the situation that prevailed during the last war when Germany practically ran her whole regime on the lowly, humble potato and its by-products. They made many things from the potato, and I would think that if we had the research committee that is proposed here today, possibly something similar could be developed from wheat, which is in great surplus in this country at the present time. It is quite conceivable that many products could be made from wheat if the time, the money and the research went into this major problem. It is not many years ago that casein was developed from milk, and from casein they made plastic, and from plastic has developed many, many products.
So I would think, Mr. Speaker, that with the co-ordination of a research committee such as proposed it would go a long way toward helping us develop some other products from our surplus agricultural products. It is generally realized, I believe, that even with the great increase in population and the rising living standards, Canada can produce more than it consumes for many years to come. I think of the field of plant pathology, where many new and better


varieties could be propagated in order to produce for Canada some of those products which we are now importing from other countries. I think of the large amount of vegetable oil which comes into Canada from the United States from which we make margarine. I think the field of research could develop suitable varieties from which we could get these vegetable oils. It was that great president of the United States, Abraham Lincoln, who once said that if we buy goods from other countries, they have the money and we have the goods; but if we produce the goods at home or grow the crops, then we have both the goods and the money. It was on that principle, along with the building of a great population, that the United States is now one of the greatest countries in the world.
I think that is a model which we should be inclined to follow more, and with a research committee we could direct our thoughts along these lines. I think that such a committee, if established, would go a long way toward co-ordinating the field of agricultural research. We have across Canada, as you know Mr. Speaker, many experimental farms and also many agricultural colleges. Each is very sincere in developing experimental work, but I think we lack very much a co-ordination between these two great bodies, the agricultural colleges and the experimental farms. If they would coordinate this research it would do away with the great waste of time and money which we have today.

subtopic: RADIATION LEVELS IN CANADA
RADIATION LEVELS IN CANADA
speechtext:
1.	What radiation levels have been reported in Canada following nuclear bomb tests (in roentgen units for comparison) for each of the last four years?
2. What is the minimum lethal dose (in roentgens)?
3. What is the supposed tolerable level (in roentgens) ?
4.	Is there any disagreement among scientists concerning (a) the minimum lethal dose; (b) the supposed tolerable level?
5.	If so, what are the nature of their contentions, and the names and qualifications of the scientists who made such statements?
Answer by: Hon. J. W. Monteith (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
1.	Direct measurements of radiation levels in Canada following nuclear bomb tests have not been made because the daily and seasonal variations in the natural background radiation levels are greater than the slight increases produced by nuclear test explosions.
Rough calculations of radiation levels can be made by making certain assumptions and using measurements of the level of radioactivity in air and in rainfall and snow. Such calculations are not being carried out on a routine basis because of the large uncertainties involved. However based on computations for Ottawa rainfall the radiation exposure due to weapon tests is estimated to be 1 per cent or less of that from natural sources, cosmic and terrestrial.
2.	A lethal dose for the individual is not defined, but it is generally agreed that a dose of about 400-500 roentgens will cause death among 50 per cent of the group exposed. However, this dose has to be delivered rapidly. For small doses given over a long period of time, the corresponding figure would be much higher.
3.	For workers using radioactive materials an exposure of 5 roentgens per year, but not exceeding 60 roentgens before the age of 30 and not exceeding 200 roentgens per lifetime exposure, is considered acceptable.
4.	(a) There is no major disagreement with regard to the range of lethal doses.

(b)	There is no major disagreement with regard to the maximum permissible exposure for workers using radioactive materials. There is disagreement with respect to the possible consequences of low levels of exposure to whole populations. The degree of uncertainty with regard to the effects of low levels of radiation upon exposed individuals has been very clearly stated in the report of the United Nations Scientific committee on the effects of atomic radiation.
5.	The nature of the possible difference of opinion has been indicated recently in an exchange of letters which has appeared in the pages of the Sunday edition of the New York Times, between Professors Linus Pauling and Barclay Kamb of the California Institute of Technology and Dr. Miriam P. Finkle of the Argonne national laboratory. The opposing contentions in this case related to whether it is likely that there is a threshold level of radiation below which there would be no effects at all even in large populations, or alternatively whether there may be very slight effects upon the incidence of leukaemia and bone tumours, which, in view of a world population of two and a half billion people, might nevertheless affect substantial numbers of individuals in the world as a whole. Professors Linus Pauling and Barclay Kamb are respectively professor of chemistry and assistant professor of geology at the California Institute of Technology. Dr. Miriam P. Finkle is in the division of biological and medical research of the Argonne national laboratory.

TRAINING OP MUSEUM CURATORS
speechtext:
1.	What facilities are there in Canada for the training of museum curators and other museum staff?
2.	What facilties in Canada are being used for the training of museum curators and other museum staff?
3.	What is the function, and what are the duties and responsibilities of a museum curator?
Answer by: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister
of Northern Affairs and National
Resources):
1.	The national museum has sponsored a week-long seminar-and proposes to sponsor others-for the training of museum curators. The national gallery has a scheme for the training of curators for art museums whereby the trainee receives instruction for an entire school year. Week-long seminars for museum curators are sponsored by the Canadian museum association. These have been held at Jordan, Ontario, at Halifax and at Victoria, and they are arranged by the regional museum leaders of the association. The association also sponsors week end "workshops" which have been held in a number of centres. Workshops are also sponsored by the Ontario historical society, principally for the curators of small historical museums. Members of the Canadian museums association are eligible to undertake home studies for the certificate of the museums association of Great Britain, and several members are currently enrolled in this scheme.
With respect to the training of museum staff other than curators, most of the larger museums in Canada accept individuals who are willing to be employed without pay on an apprenticeship basis with the object of learning the techniques and methods of museum work. The national museum of Canada and the Royal Ontario museum have accepted trainees on this basis, some of whom have been supported by museums sponsoring them and others by grants from the Canada Council.
2.	See answer to No. 1.
3.	One of the main responsibilities of a museum curator is to preserve and exhibit (as may be appropriate) the contents of the museum or museum section for which he is responsible. The duties and responsibilities vary greatly according to the type of museum concerned, its size and the nature of its contents. They also vary with the emphasis placed on the various phases of the museum's activities. A curator of a large museum normally acquires specimens to add to the museum's collections, studies them, records data about them and supervises
their storage and preservation. He supervises the preparation of exhibits displaying them to the public, and explains their significance by the production of scientific reports and papers, which are publicized in scientific and popular periodicals and by means of lectures, radio, television and other media.

2.	On what date was this done, and by what legal instrument were these positions authorized?
Answer by: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister
of Northern Affairs and National
Resources):
1 and 2. Pursuant to section 9 of the Civil Service Act and under the authority of the Financial Administration Act, the position of director, national museum of Canada was established and approved by treasury board minute 503905 of May 18, 1956. The then government later decided to seek legislation to divide the national museum into a museum of natural history and a museum of human history and decided to create an additional position of director. This additional position was recommended under the Civil Service Act, concurred in by treasury board and approved by the governor in council effective December 28, 1956 as shown in a supplementary list of positions.

C.N.R. CLEANING PLANT
speechtext:
1.	Is the Canadian National Railways planning a cleaning plant at either Port Arthur or Neebing?
2.	If so, when will this plant go into operation, what will be its capacity, and how many men will be required to man the plant?
3.	How is such cleaning work being carried on at the present time, and how many men are involved?
Questions
4.	Will the new cleaning plant have any effect upon the work being done at the Port Arthur repair tracks?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of
Transport):
The management of the Canadian National Railways advise as follows:
1.	A car cleaning track has been constructed at Port Arthur.
2.	The plant will go into operation this spring. The capacity of the track is approximately 150 cars. Estimated cleaning staff will be approximately 15 and an additional 10 engaged in making light repairs and upgrading cars.
3.	Cars are now being cleaned for paper loading at Neebing, for paper and flour loading at Port Arthur, and for general freight on the freight shed tracks. Eleven men are now engaged in this work. Two men are also employed at Port Arthur and two at Neebing engaged in light repairs to cars which are being cleaned.
4.	The men engaged in the light repairs on the new cleaning track will be under the jurisdiction of the Port Arthur repair track foreman and will not result in a decrease in the Port Arthur repair track staff.

speakerposition: subtopic

DR. RICHARD S. MACNEISH-NATIONAL MUSEUM APPOINTMENT
speechtext:
1.	On what date was Dr. Richard S. MacNeish first appointed to the staff of the national museum of Canada, and to what position was he appointed?
2.	Did this position come under the Civil Service Act and regulations?
3.	Was this position advertised by a civil service competition?
4.	If so, (a) Did Dr. MacNeish apply? (b) What was the position advertised for, and the date it was advertised? (c) What names appeared on the civil service eligibility list? (d) In what order were the names listed? (e) How many persons applied? (f) What was the closing date for the receipt of applications?
5.	Was Dr. MacNeish a British subject or Canadian citizen at the time he applied for this position?
6.	If not, has the civil service commission been notified that he had applied for naturalization papers either as a British subject or Canadian citizen by the closing date for the receipt of applications for this competition?
7.	If not, on what authority was Dr. MacNeish permitted to compete in this examination?
Answer by:	Hon. Henri Courlemanche
(Secretary of State):
1.	Dr. Richard S. MacNeish was first appointed to the staff of the national museum of Canada on June 20, 1949. He was appointed to position, MR-MMU-5 as an anthropologist 3.
2.	Yes.
3.	Yes.
4.	(a) Yes.
(b)	This position had become vacant and, since it was considered that no one in civil service possessed the qualifications required, it was advertised as an open competition on March 30, 1949.
(c)	The name of Dr. MacNeish was the only name on the eligible list for this competition.
(d)	See (c).
(e)	Two.
(f)	April 23, 1949.
5.	No.
6.	The civil service commission had not been notified that Dr. MacNeish had applied for naturalization papers as a British subject or a Canadian citizen by the closing date for the receipt of applications in this competition,
7.	Dr. MacNeish's application was admitted to competition 49-4450 by authority of P.C. 24/3539 of July 15, 1949, which exempted him from the requirements of section 33 (1), now 32 (1), of the Civil Service Act. This section of the Civil Service Act reads as follows:
"No person shall, without the authority of the governor in council, be admitted to any examination unless he is a natural born or naturalized British subject and also has been a resident of Canada or Newfoundland for at least five years."
